textbookText: Activity: 1.3.1 Explore mitosis creating temporary and permanent slides. Objective: Study of mitosis in onion root tips cells by preparing temporary slides and permanent slides.

Part 1 | Growing Onion Roots | Day 1 – 5 Objective 1: Observe and document the growth of roots in an onion using a simple water-based method. Materials: Fresh onion, toothpicks, transparent glass, water.
Procedure: - Insert toothpicks around the middle of the onion. - Place the onion, supported by toothpicks, in a half-filled glass of water.

Part 2 | Preparation and microscopic Observation of Onion Root Tip | Day 6 Objective 2: Prepare a temporary microscopic slide from a newly grown onion root, observe its cellular structure, and attempt to identify stages of mitosis.
Materials: Just grown roots of onion, blade, microscope slides, coverslips, microscope, safranin. Procedure:

- Gently pluck a young root from the just grown onion. - Place a small section of the root on a watch glass. - Add a few drops of safranin for a few seconds and wash with water. - Cut a few thin slices (T/S) of the dyed root. - Now, place them on a glass slide and cover
with a coverslip. - Observe under the microscope. Observation: Examine cells of the root tip under low (10x – 40x) and high (100x using immersion oil) magnifications.
- Note any visible structures, patterns, or characteristics.

3. REDUCTIONALCELLDIVISION OR MEIOSIS (G., meioum = to lessen; osis = state) It is the type of cell division in which a mature diploid mother cell divides into four haploid daughter cells. Since the number of chromosomes in daughter cells is reduced to half, it is also called reductional cell division. For the first time, meiosis was discovered and described by Oscar Hertwig in sea urchin eggs (1876).
Do you know? Meiosis was first demonstrated by Belgian embryologist Edouard Van Benden (1883) in Ascaris roundworm eggs. The term "meiosis" was given by Farmer and Moore (1905).

Meiosis does not always occur in all cells, but in special types of cells like germ cells, pollen mother cells, megaspore mother cells when they are to undergo sexual reproduction. The cells that undergo meiosis are called meiocytes. Interphase is observed prior to cell division, like in mitosis. However, G2 phase is either short or absent in this type. Meiosis is a double cell division comprising: Meiosis I and meiosis II. The transition between these phases is short and without DNA replication. It is called interkinesis. Meiosis I Meiosis-I forms two daughter cells each bearing the half number of chromosomes than their mother cell. It is divided into:

A. Karyokinesis-I B. Cytokinesis-I. A. Karyokinesis-I It involves the division of nucleus in four distinct phases: Prophase-I: This phase is complex and long which is simplified into five successive subphases. i. Leptotene or Leptonema ii. Zygotene or Zygonema iii. Pachytene or Pachynema iv. Diplotene or Diplonema v. Diakinesis i. Leptotene (G., 'leptos' = thin; 'tene' = thread): Leptotene stage, also known as the thinthreaded stage, is characterized by following key events: b. The nucleus enlarges. c. The chromosomes become long and visible in the form of single-stranded threads called chromomeres due to condensation, thickening and shortening. d. The chromosomes' arrangement forms a bouquet at one side of the nucleus, known as the bouquet stage. e. The nuclear membrane and nucleolus remain intact.

vi. Zygotene (G., 'zygo' = yoke; 'nema' = thread): Zygotene stage, also known as yokedthreaded or Zygonema stage is characterized by following key events: a. Shorter, thicker, and coiled homologous chromosomes from the father and mother pair forming bivalents through a process called synapsis. b. Asters continue to move away from each other.

Fig. 1.3.3 Zygotene i. Pachytene (G., 'pachys' = thick; 'nema' = thread): The thick-threaded stage, also called pachynema, is relatively longer than Leptotene and Zygotene stages. It is characterized by following key events: a. During this stage, the bivalents become shorter and thicker, and each homologous chromosome splits along its length, except in the centromere region forming two chromatids. b. Each synaptonemal pair is called a bivalent or dyad because it comprises two visible chromosomes. Alternatively, it can be termed a quadrivalent or tetrad due to the presence of four visible chromatids. The two chromatids of the same chromosome are called sister chromatids. c. Crossing-over occurs, involving the exchange of chromatid segments between nonsister chromatids of each tetrad, and the locations where crossing-over happens are termed chiasmata (singular: chiasma).
